caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (설치 서비스를 함께 하는 동네 가전 매장) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: '너무 비싸다'는 판결이 아니라 비교다. 무엇과 비교하는지 알아내면 가격을 깎지 않고도 대화를 이어갈 수 있다.
misconception: '비싸다'는 말이 나오면 할인을 해 주거나, 제품이 왜 좋은지 더 길게 설명해야 한다.

sources.text: 영업 실무의 일반 원칙 (가격 이의 다루기: 비교 대상 확인, 같은 조건 비교, 가격 대신 범위 조정, 정직한 긴급성)
모든 인물, 매장, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 설치 포함 견적 $1,850 − 온라인 본체 가격 $1,450 = $400 차이. 예산 $1,500에 맞춰 깎으면 $1,850 − $1,500 = $350 손실. 40갤런 설치 포함 $1,590은 가상 가격.
'탱크 바닥의 녹은 누수 위험 신호'라는 내용은 일반적인 정비 상식으로 썼습니다. 특정 수명이나 고장 확률 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
설치 허가 등 특정 국가 규정은 언급하지 않았습니다. 포함 항목은 설치, 기존 탱크 수거, 새 부품, 1년 시공 보증으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: 'Too expensive' compared to what?
body: You run a family appliance store that also installs what it sells. On Saturday morning, Maria comes in. Her water heater is twelve years old and the water keeps running lukewarm.
You quote **$1,850**, installed. She looks at the paper, then at her phone, and says: "That's too expensive."
The next four decisions are yours.

image.label: Customer at a store counter holding up her phone
image.brief: 따뜻한 톤의 동네 가전 매장 카운터. 뒤편에 온수기 몇 대. 중년 여성 고객이 견적서를 한 손에, 휴대폰을 다른 손에 들고 있고 카운터 너머 주인이 듣고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your first words.
body: Maria has just said "That's too expensive." She hasn't walked away yet. What do you say?

options.text: "I can take 10% off for you today."
options.feedback: She may say yes, but you just gave away $185 without knowing what bothered her. And she learns your first price wasn't real.

options.text: "Fair enough. What are you comparing it to?"
options.feedback: You stay calm and find out what "expensive" means to her. She turns her phone around: the same model online for $1,450.

options.text: "This model is very efficient. Let me show you the specs."
options.feedback: The facts may be true, but you're answering a question she didn't ask. She nods politely and starts drifting toward the door.

cards.title: The $400 gap.
body: Say you chose B. The online listing is the same model for **$1,450**. Unit only, delivery extra, installation not included.
Your $1,850 covers installation, hauling away the old tank, new fittings and a one-year guarantee on the work. What now?

options.text: Match the online price to keep the sale
options.feedback: You'd be doing the installation for free. You keep Maria, but every future customer with a phone can ask for the same.

options.text: Put both offers side by side, line by line
options.feedback: Now she sees she isn't comparing like with like. To match your quote online, she'd still need delivery, a plumber and somewhere to dump the old tank.

options.text: Warn her that online sellers are unreliable
options.feedback: It sounds defensive, and she may know people who bought online just fine. You lose trust without closing the gap.

cards.callout: "Too expensive" is usually a comparison. Your job is to make it a fair one.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the comparison is often a cheaper tool or a spreadsheet. Ask what they're comparing against, then compare the full cost: setup, training, the hours someone spends keeping the spreadsheet alive.

cards.title: "I get it. But I budgeted $1,500."
body: Say you chose B. Maria agrees your offer is fairer than she thought. Her budget is still her budget.
She mentions she lives with one other person. You also stock a smaller 40-gallon model, installed for **$1,590**. What do you offer?

options.feedback: You lose $350 on the job and teach her that pushing works. Next time she'll push harder.

options.text: Offer the smaller model, fully installed, at $1,590
options.feedback: You change what she gets, not what it's worth. She stays close to budget, and your price stays honest.

options.text: Offer to split the $1,850 into monthly payments
options.feedback: It can help with cash flow, but it doesn't answer the budget she set. Some customers feel pushed into spending more than they planned.

cards.title: "Let me think about it."
body: Say you chose B. Maria likes the smaller model. Then she pauses: "Let me talk it over at home."
Earlier, you noticed rust around the base of her old tank in the photo she showed you. What do you say?

options.feedback: If it isn't true, she'll find out when she calls back next week. Fake urgency can win one sale and lose a customer for good.

options.text: Mention the rust, hold the quote for 30 days, and offer to call Thursday
options.feedback: The reason to act soon is real and it's hers, not yours. She leaves with a clear next step and no pressure.
Polite and safe, but it leaves her with no next step. Busy weeks swallow good intentions.

cards.title: A price objection is a comparison, not a verdict.
body: On Thursday, Maria books the installation. You never lowered a price.

"Too expensive" rarely means "worthless." It means *more than something else*: a website, a budget, a rival's quote, or doing nothing. Once you know the comparison, you can check if it's fair, change the scope, or give an honest reason to decide.
**Ask before you answer.** Discounts and speeches both skip that step.

image.label: Two quotes side by side with matching line items
image.brief: 견적서 두 장을 나란히 놓은 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Online $1,450"에는 본체만 체크, 나머지 "Delivery, Installation, Old tank removal, Fittings, 1-year guarantee"는 빈칸. 오른쪽 "Store $1,850"에는 모든 항목 체크. 실제 상표 없음.

cards.title: Sometimes the price really is too high for them.
body: None of this is a trick for getting every yes. If the fair comparison still shows the other offer is better for this customer, say so.
A customer who hears "honestly, the online unit plus a handyman may suit you" often comes back for the next job, and sends friends.
And if you can't trade scope without cutting quality, don't. A cheaper job done badly costs more trust than a lost sale.

cards.title: Find the comparison before you defend the price.
body: **Try it today:** think of the last time a customer said "too expensive." Write down what they were really comparing you to.
list: **Decision 1:** ask what "expensive" is measured against (Price objections)
**Decision 2:** compare like with like (Looking at a competitor)
**Decision 4:** give a real reason to act, not a fake deadline (Honest urgency, 'Not right now')
